title: Fremont County CO wells and drilling cost
meta_description: In Fremont County, Colorado, the median well depth is 182 ft and the median yield is 7 gpm. See what that means for drilling cost and water reliability.
h1: Water wells in Fremont County, Colorado
intro_html:
In Fremont County you’re in classic mountain country: most wells are tapping fractured bedrock, not a big sand aquifer. That means well depth and yield can change a lot over short distances, from Cañon City and Penrose up toward Cotopaxi and Coaldale.

County-wide records from the Colorado Division of Water Resources give a good picture of what’s typical here: how deep most wells go, how much water they make, and what a new well is likely to cost in this terrain.

sections.heading: How deep Fremont County wells usually go
sections.html:
Across Fremont County, the median reported well depth is 182 feet, with the middle half running from 80 to 320 feet. About 29% of wells are under 100 feet, 39% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 26% run 300 to 600 feet, and 6% go past 600 feet. The deepest on record is 3,216 feet.

For bids, I’d assume your well will likely land somewhere in that 80–320 foot band, but be ready for the possibility of a 300–600 foot hole, especially in higher, rocky ground away from areas like Cañon City, Penrose, and Florence. In fractured bedrock, two lots a quarter mile apart can end up with very different depths.

sections.heading: Well yield in fractured Fremont County bedrock
sections.html:
Out of the wells that report production, the median yield is 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 4.5 and 10.0 gpm. Only about 3% of wells come in under 1 gpm, 22% are between 1 and 5 gpm, 61% fall in the 5 to 15 gpm range, and 14% exceed 15 gpm.

For a single household on an exempt domestic well, a 4–10 gpm well is usually workable when paired with decent storage and plumbing. The low share of sub‑1 gpm wells is encouraging, but that risk is not zero. In this kind of fractured‑bedrock aquifer, small changes in geology can mean your neighbor’s 10 gpm does not guarantee your lot will match it.

sections.heading: Water levels and long-term trend here
sections.html:
Static water levels in Fremont County show a median of 85 feet below ground, with the middle half between 50 and 160 feet. Looking by decade, median depth to water has shifted from about 38 feet in the 1970s to 45 feet in the 1980s, then deeper around 90 feet in the 1990s. It improved somewhat to the 80–85 foot range in the 2000s and 2010s, then dipped deeper again to about 100 feet in the 2020s.

That pattern suggests water is generally farther down now than in the 1970s and 1980s. Practically, you plan for more pumping lift and power use than the old timers had, and you don’t assume future wells will be as shallow as older ones on nearby parcels.

sections.heading: Who has been drilling in Fremont County, and when
sections.html:
Fremont County has a long drilling history, with 10,255 wells in state records and 6,637 marked as constructed. Permits took off in the 1970s and 1980s, with 927 and 1,192 permits respectively. Activity peaked in the 1990s with 2,460 permits, stayed strong in the 2000s at 2,171, then eased to 1,133 in the 2010s and 858 so far in the 2020s. The newest permit on record is from 2026.

Most wells are for domestic or household use at 83%, with stock wells at 19%, a small 1% for irrigation, and 9% for monitoring. The vast majority target an unnamed fractured‑bedrock aquifer, with only a handful tagged Alluvial or Dakota. Active drillers include Arkansas Valley Drilling (Moore, Todd A.), American Drilling Service (Dewberry, Bradford W.), and Finney Drilling (Finney, Larry D.).

sections.heading: What a new Fremont County well is likely to cost
sections.html:
In Fremont County’s fractured granite and gneiss, typical drilling rates run about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s median depth of 182 feet, that puts the bare drilled hole around $11,800–$18,200. Once you add a pump, pressure tank, trenching to the house, and electrical work, a complete well system at that depth usually runs about $17,800–$30,200.

If you end up in that 300–600 foot group instead of right at the median, the per‑foot cost multiplies quickly. When comparing land around places like Cotopaxi, Coaldale, or Canon City, ask for nearby well logs so you’re budgeting off local depths instead of just the county-wide median.

sections.heading: Risks to check: low yield, contamination, and siting
sections.html:
Only 3% of reported wells produce under 1 gpm, but that’s still a real risk when you’re buying a vacant parcel. Have a driller or pump contractor review nearby well logs for depth and yield before you commit. Fractured bedrock can also give you variable water quality, so a lab test on an existing well is smart due diligence.

Within about 10 miles there are 14 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 404 historic mine features, and 20 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That doesn’t mean your specific well is bad, but it does mean you take water testing seriously and pay attention to where septic, wells, and old mine workings sit relative to each other on your lot.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Fremont County well lot
sections.html:
Most Fremont County domestic wells are exempt household wells, limited in how much they can pump and where that water can be used. Plan your home, garden, and any livestock around those legal limits, not just what your pump can deliver. In over‑appropriated basins nearby, some new uses can require augmentation; it’s worth confirming the exact well permit conditions with the Colorado DWR.

For vacant land near places like Florence, Brookside, or Park Center, make your contract contingent on confirming well rights and realistic drilling depth. On an existing home, pull the well record, confirm the reported yield (median is 7.0 gpm here), and consider a pump test if the system is older or has a shallow recovery level.

faq.q: How deep are domestic wells in Fremont County, Colorado?
faq.a: In Fremont County, the median reported well depth is 182 feet, with the middle half of wells between 80 and 320 feet. About 29% are under 100 feet, 39% are 100–300 feet, 26% run 300–600 feet, and 6% go deeper than 600 feet. Local geology and elevation around places like Cañon City, Penrose, and Cotopaxi will push you toward the shallow or deep end of that range.

faq.q: How much water do Fremont County wells usually produce?
faq.a: Based on 3,276 wells that report pump yield, the median production in Fremont County is 7.0 gpm, with the middle half between 4.5 and 10.0 gpm. Only about 3% of wells report under 1 gpm, 22% fall between 1 and 5 gpm, 61% are 5–15 gpm, and 14% exceed 15 gpm. For a typical exempt domestic well, that 4–10 gpm band is normally enough with proper storage.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a water well in Fremont County, CO?
faq.a: In Fremont County’s fractured mountain bedrock, drilling typically runs about $65–$100 per foot. At the county median depth of 182 feet, that means roughly $11,800–$18,200 for the drilled hole. A complete system with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical usually totals around $17,800–$30,200 at that depth. Deeper wells in the 300–600 foot range scale up from there.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Fremont County, Colorado?
faq.a: Water quality varies by location and depth. Most Fremont County wells tap a fractured‑bedrock aquifer, with a few in alluvial and Dakota units. Within about 10 miles there are 14 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 404 historic mine features, and 20 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those regional numbers mean testing is important; a well-specific lab analysis is the only way to know if a given domestic well is safe.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping in Fremont County wells?
faq.a: Median static water levels have generally deepened compared to the 1970s. Median depth to water was about 38 feet in the 1970s, 45 feet in the 1980s, around 90 feet in the 1990s, then improved to roughly 85 and 80 feet in the 2000s and 2010s, and about 100 feet in the 2020s. That history suggests water is usually farther down now than in the 1970s–1980s, so plan for more pumping lift.
